questions.question: To protect patient privacy, a hospital's security team restricts its records system so tightly that night-shift emergency doctors cannot open charts. Which security goal is this change MOST directly harming?

options.A: Confidentiality, because fewer people can now read the records
options.B: Integrity, because records may now change without approval
options.C: Availability, because authorized staff cannot reach records in time
options.D: Non-repudiation, because doctors can now deny opening the records

questions.key_concept: Availability means authorized users can reach data when needed; over-tight confidentiality controls can harm it.
questions.pre_read: Ask what actually went wrong for the people involved: did data leak, change, or become unreachable?
questions.correct_explanation: Availability means authorized people can use systems and data when they need them. Emergency doctors are authorized, yet the new restriction stops them opening charts, so availability is harmed, and in a hospital that can put patients at risk. Confidentiality is the goal the change was meant to protect; it is strengthened here, not harmed. Good security balances the three goals for each asset.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the change is about who may read records. But tighter access strengthens confidentiality; the harm is that authorized doctors are blocked.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because records are at stake. But integrity fails when data is altered without authorization; here nothing changes, and staff simply cannot open charts.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the change concerns who opens records. But non-repudiation proves who did something; here the problem is that doctors are blocked from charts.

tips: Eliminate: B describes altered data and D describes deniable actions; neither happens when doctors simply cannot open charts.
Final two: C beats A because the restriction protects confidentiality but blocks authorized doctors, and blocked access is an availability failure that can endanger patients.
Exam cue: name the goal by the harm. Disclosure hurts confidentiality, alteration hurts integrity, and authorized users being blocked hurts availability.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-12 Rev. 1 Section 1.4 (Important Terminology: confidentiality, integrity, availability)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1.1.1 The CIA Triad (goals can conflict; exam trap 'security should always maximize confidentiality'). Original hospital night-shift scenario written for KaiSip; no ISC2 training, CBK or prep-bank text used. CC pilot batch, Oct 2026. Review fixes 28 Oct 2026 (blind test and standards audit): calibrated cues, teaching fields and pre_read.

questions.question: A courier firm wants proof that each driver confirmed each delivery, so that no driver can later credibly deny it. Which approach BEST provides this?

options.A: Each driver signs confirmations with their own private key
options.B: Confirmations are encrypted with one key the drivers share
options.C: Each confirmation is stored with a plain hash to detect changes
options.D: Confirmations carry a keyed hash using a key shared with the depot

questions.key_concept: Non-repudiation needs proof tied to one person, such as a digital signature made with their private key.
questions.pre_read: Look at what each option uses to mark a confirmation. Then picture a driver later denying one.
questions.correct_explanation: Non-repudiation needs evidence tied to one person. A digital signature is made with a private key that only its holder controls, and anyone can check it with the matching public key, so the driver cannot credibly say someone else confirmed the delivery. A keyed hash proves a key holder made the message, but the depot holds the same key, so either side could have produced it.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because encryption feels like strong protection. But it mainly keeps content secret, and a key the drivers share cannot show which driver sent anything.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because a hash does detect changes. But a plain hash uses no key, so anyone can compute it, and it says nothing about who confirmed.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: a keyed hash proves a key holder made it. But the depot shares that key, so the driver could claim the depot created the record.

tips: Eliminate: B uses encryption, which keeps content secret but proves no sender, and C uses a plain hash, which detects change but carries no key.
Final two: A beats D because a shared key leaves two possible authors; only a private key held by one person gives non-repudiation.
Exam cue: for 'cannot deny' questions, look for something only one person controls, such as a private signing key; anything shared weakens the proof.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AU-10 (Non-repudiation); NIST SP 800-12 Rev. 1 Section 9.1.3 (Electronic Signatures)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1.1.7 Non-Repudiation (shared secrets cannot give non-repudiation), with the plain hash vs keyed hash distinction from 1.1.3. Original courier delivery scenario written for KaiSip; no ISC2 training, CBK or prep-bank text used. CC pilot batch, Oct 2026. questions.question: Five receptionists at a veterinary clinic share one login for the booking system, and appointments were deleted overnight. Which change should the office manager approve to BEST restore accountability?

options.A: Require a longer, more complex password for the shared login
options.B: Limit the shared login to viewing appointments, not deleting them
options.C: Turn on more detailed logging for the shared booking account
options.D: Give each receptionist a separate login for the booking system

questions.key_concept: Accountability needs a unique identity for each person, so logged actions trace to one individual.
questions.pre_read: Picture the log entry after the deletion. Ask what it can and cannot tell the manager.
questions.correct_explanation: Accountability means tracing each action to one responsible person. With a shared login, the logs can record what happened but never who did it. Separate logins let accounting tie every deletion to a named receptionist. More detailed logging is the tempting runner-up, but richer logs of a shared account still cannot tell five people apart.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because a stronger password improves authentication. But all five still sign in as one identity, so their actions stay untraceable.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because limiting rights is authorization and can reduce damage. But receptionists still need to manage bookings, and the logs would still not show who acted.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because logging is the accounting step. But extra detail about one shared account still cannot name which of the five people acted.

tips: Eliminate: A strengthens authentication and B narrows authorization; neither changes the fact that five people act under one identity.
Final two: D beats C because logging only gives accountability when each identity belongs to one person; detailed logs of a shared login still name nobody.
Exam cue: when logs cannot name who acted, look for unique accounts first. Accounting records actions; accountability also needs one person per identity.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 IA-2 (Identification and Authentication (Organizational Users)); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AU-2 (Event Logging)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1.1.6 Authorization and Accounting (accountability needs unique accounts; with a shared login nobody knows who acted). Original veterinary clinic scenario written for KaiSip; no ISC2 training, CBK or prep-bank text used. CC pilot batch, Oct 2026. questions.question: A city council team is building an AI chatbot for residents' tax questions and plans to keep every full chat transcript indefinitely for future training. What should the security analyst raise FIRST?

options.A: Whether the stored transcripts will be encrypted while at rest
options.B: Whether that much personal data is needed, and for how long
options.C: Whether rate limits stop the chatbot from being overloaded
options.D: Whether each chatbot action is logged under a named account

questions.key_concept: Privacy by design limits personal data to what the purpose needs and sets how long it is kept, before adding safeguards.
questions.pre_read: Notice what the plan collects from residents and what happens to it afterward. Ask what a resident would want to know.
questions.correct_explanation: Privacy by design starts by asking what personal data a purpose truly needs and how long to keep it. Tax chats hold residents' personal details, and keeping all of them indefinitely breaks data minimization and retention limits. Encryption is worth adding, but it only protects secrecy; it cannot make unneeded collection or endless retention acceptable. The data owner then decides what is kept.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because encryption protects stored personal data. But it answers who can read the data, not whether it should be collected and kept at all.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because public chatbots can draw heavy traffic. But rate limits protect availability; the concern here is how much personal data is kept.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because logging each AI action supports accountability. But it does not address keeping more personal data than the purpose needs.

tips: Eliminate: C protects availability and D supports accountability; the problem in this plan is how much personal data is kept, and for how long.
Final two: B beats A because privacy first asks whether data should be collected and kept; encryption only protects data that perhaps should not exist.
Exam cue: when a design keeps personal data 'just in case', think data minimization and retention limits before any technical safeguard.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 SA-8(33) (Security and Privacy Engineering Principles | Minimization); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 SI-12(1) (Information Management and Retention | Limit Personally Identifiable Information Elements)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1.1.8 Privacy and Personal Data (data minimization, retention, exam trap 'if personal data is encrypted, privacy is taken care of') and 1.1.9 AI and the Core Security Concepts (personal data in training data). questions.question: A school's IT team patches a flaw in its public web server that a criminal group is actively exploiting at other schools. What does the patch MOST directly change?

options.A: It removes the threat the criminal group poses to the school
options.B: It removes the vulnerability the criminal group could exploit
options.C: It transfers the remaining risk to the software vendor
options.D: It lowers the value of the web server as an asset

questions.key_concept: A threat is a possible cause of harm; a vulnerability is a weakness it uses. Patching reduces the vulnerability, not the threat.
questions.pre_read: Separate the attackers, the weakness and the harm in the scenario. Ask which of these the patch actually touches.
questions.correct_explanation: A vulnerability is a weakness a threat can use; a threat is whoever or whatever could cause harm. Patching fixes the server's weakness, so this route of attack closes. The criminal group still exists and may look for another weakness, which is why the patch does not remove the threat. Organizations lower risk mainly by reducing vulnerabilities and impact, because they rarely control threats.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the attack stops working. But the criminal group still exists and can try other weaknesses; patching removes the weakness, not the attacker.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the vendor supplied the fix. But transfer shifts financial impact to another party, such as an insurer; installing a patch is the school's own mitigation.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because risk does depend on what is at stake. But a patch changes the server's weakness, not what the server is worth to the school.

tips: Eliminate: C confuses patching with transfer, which shifts costs to another party, and D confuses risk with asset value, which a patch does not change.
Final two: B beats A because a patch fixes the weakness; the attackers, the threat, still exist and may try another route.
Exam cue: you rarely control threats. Controls such as patching shrink vulnerabilities or impact, and that is how risk goes down.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-30 Rev. 1 Section 2.3.1 (Risk Models: threats, vulnerabilities, likelihood and impact); NIST CSF 2.0 ID.RA-01 (vulnerabilities in assets are identified, validated and recorded); NIST CSF 2.0 ID.RA-03 (internal and external threats to the organization are identified and recorded)

questions.question: A parent portal's residual risk, owned by the school district's IT director, is within tolerance, and the project lead asks a security analyst to sign the acceptance. What should the analyst do FIRST?

options.A: Sign the acceptance and copy the risk owner
options.B: Hold the launch until the residual risk is gone
options.C: Document the risk and route the acceptance to the risk owner
options.D: Escalate the acceptance to the school board for sign-off

questions.key_concept: Only the risk owner accepts residual risk, and only within tolerance; the practitioner documents it and routes it there.
questions.pre_read: Notice who is asking, who is being asked to sign, and who owns the risk.
questions.correct_explanation: Accepting risk commits the organization, so only someone with that authority may do it: within tolerance, the risk owner, here the IT director. The analyst's role is to document the residual risk clearly and route the acceptance to that owner. Signing and then copying the owner is the tempting runner-up, but the analyst would still be making the owner's decision.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the risk owner is told. But being told is not deciding; the analyst's signature would commit the organization without authority.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because removing all risk sounds safest. But controls rarely remove all risk; risk within tolerance can be formally accepted instead.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the board sits at the top. But boards set risk appetite rather than signing each acceptance; within tolerance, the risk owner decides.

tips: Eliminate: B expects zero residual risk, which controls rarely reach, and D sends a within-tolerance risk to the board, which sets appetite rather than signing each acceptance.
Final two: C beats A because only the risk owner may accept the risk; copying the owner after signing still leaves the analyst making the decision.
Exam cue: when asked to accept or sign off a risk, document it and route it to the risk owner; tolerance decides whether that owner or senior leadership signs.
questions.framework_ref: ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Clause 6.1.3 f) (risk owners approve the risk treatment plan and accept residual risk); NIST CSF 2.0 GV.RM-02 (risk appetite and risk tolerance statements are established, communicated and maintained)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1.2.6 Risk Appetite, Tolerance and Acceptance (practitioners never accept risk; within tolerance the risk owner accepts, above it senior management decides). questions.question: A $60,000 server loses 25% of its value in a flood, expected once every 5 years. If flood protection costs $5,000 a year, which finding is MOST accurate to report to the risk owner?

options.A: Yearly loss averages $3,000, so protection costs more than it saves
options.B: One flood would cost $15,000, so protection is clearly worthwhile
options.C: The server is worth $60,000, so protection is clearly worthwhile
options.D: Protection costs too much, so the analyst accepts the risk

questions.key_concept: Annualized loss expectancy (ALE) is single loss expectancy (SLE) times the annualized rate of occurrence (ARO); compare it with a control's yearly cost.
questions.pre_read: Work out the cost of one flood, then spread it over the years between floods. Check each option's numbers and its claim.
questions.correct_explanation: Single loss expectancy is $60,000 × 25% = $15,000. A flood once every 5 years gives an annualized rate of occurrence of 0.2, so annualized loss expectancy is $15,000 × 0.2 = $3,000 a year. Protection costing $5,000 a year exceeds the loss it could prevent. The analyst reports this to the risk owner, who decides whether to accept the risk or treat it another way.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because $15,000 is a real figure here. But it is the single loss expectancy, one flood's cost; spread over 5 years, the yearly loss is $3,000.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the server's value sounds like what is at risk. But a flood destroys 25% of it, and only once every 5 years on average.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: the math is right. But accepting risk commits the organization, so the risk owner decides; the analyst reports the finding.

tips: Eliminate: B uses the cost of one flood, the single loss expectancy (SLE), and C uses the server's full value; neither spreads the loss over a year.
Final two: A beats D because both read the numbers correctly, but only the risk owner may accept a risk; the analyst reports the finding.
Exam cue: ALE = asset value × exposure factor × annualized rate of occurrence (ARO). Compare ALE with the control's yearly cost, then hand the decision to the risk owner.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-30 Rev. 1 Section 2.3.2 (Assessment Approaches: quantitative assessments support cost-benefit analysis of risk responses)

questions.question: After a risk assessment, a dental group buys cyber insurance, and its office manager says patient data security is now the insurer's responsibility. What is the BEST response from the security coordinator?

options.A: Agree that the insurer is now responsible for patient data security
options.B: Explain that insurance mitigates the risk, so some controls can go
options.C: Explain that insurance means the risk is accepted, so controls can stop
options.D: Explain that the group stays accountable, as insurance pays some costs

questions.key_concept: Risk transfer, such as insurance, shifts some financial impact to another party; accountability for the data stays with the organization.
questions.pre_read: Notice what the office manager believes changed when the insurance was bought. Test that belief against each option.
questions.correct_explanation: Buying insurance is risk transfer: the insurer pays some of the financial impact if a breach happens. It does not move the group's duty to protect patient data, and patients and regulators will still hold the group accountable. The manager's view is the common misreading of transfer, so the coordinator corrects it and keeps the existing controls in place.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because insurance is called risk transfer. But only financial impact moves; the group stays accountable to patients and regulators for their data.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because insurance softens the financial hit. But mitigation means controls that lower likelihood or impact; insurance pays after a loss and makes no breach less likely.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the group has chosen to live with some loss. But acceptance is the risk owner's documented decision; insurance is transfer, and it does not replace controls.

tips: Eliminate: B calls insurance mitigation and C calls it acceptance; insurance is risk transfer, and neither label justifies dropping controls.
Final two: D beats A because transfer moves some financial impact to the insurer; accountability for patient data stays with the group.
Exam cue: insurance and outsourcing can move costs or work, but not accountability. The organization still answers to customers and regulators.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 RA-7 (Risk Response); NIST CSF 2.0 ID.RA-06 (risk responses are chosen, prioritized, planned, tracked and communicated)

questions.question: A security team wants every workstation to lock its screen after 10 minutes of inactivity, across the whole company. In which document does this requirement BEST belong?

options.A: The organization's top-level information security policy
options.B: A guideline that suggests good workstation habits
options.C: A procedure listing the steps to set up a workstation
options.D: A standard that sets workstation security settings

questions.key_concept: Standards hold specific mandatory settings that support a policy; policies stay high level, and guidelines are optional.
questions.pre_read: Notice how specific the requirement is and who must follow it. Then match it to each document type.
questions.correct_explanation: Exact, mandatory settings such as a 10-minute screen lock belong in a standard, which turns policy into specifics. The top-level policy stays high level, stating what is required and why, so it is not rewritten each time a setting changes. That makes the policy the closest wrong answer: it is mandatory, but too broad for exact values. A procedure then gives the steps to apply the setting.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because policy is mandatory and approved by leaders. But policies stay high level; exact values like timeouts belong in a standard beneath them.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because screen locks are a good habit. But guidelines are optional advice, and a company-wide requirement must be mandatory.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the lock is set on each workstation. But procedures give the steps for applying a setting; they are not where the requirement is set.

tips: Eliminate: B is a guideline, which is optional, and C is a procedure, which gives steps to follow rather than setting the requirement.
Final two: D beats A because policies state intent at a high level, while exact mandatory settings such as timeouts belong in standards.
Exam cue: policy says what and why, a standard says which exact setting, a procedure says how, and a guideline only suggests.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-12 Rev. 1 Section 5.1 (Standards, Guidelines, and Procedures); ISO/IEC 27002:2022 Control 5.1 (Policies for information security)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1.3.5 Standards, Procedures and Guidelines and 1.3.4 Security Policies (exam trap 'a policy should list exact settings'). Original screen-lock requirement written for KaiSip; no ISC2 training, CBK or prep-bank text used. CC pilot batch, Oct 2026. Review fixes 28 Oct 2026 (blind test and standards audit): calibrated cues, teaching fields and pre_read.

questions.question: A sales director asks a service desk analyst to disable multifactor authentication (MFA) for a two-week trade show, though a policy owned by the IT security manager requires MFA. What should the analyst do FIRST?

options.A: Switch MFA off for two weeks on the director's approval
options.B: Swap MFA for longer passwords and inform the policy owner
options.C: Route the request to the policy owner as an exception
options.D: Refuse the request outright, since the policy makes MFA mandatory

questions.key_concept: Policy exceptions are approved, recorded and time-limited by the policy owner; practitioners route requests instead of deciding them.
questions.pre_read: Notice who is asking, who owns the policy, and what the analyst's role covers.
questions.correct_explanation: Policies are mandatory, but they allow formal exceptions that the policy owner, here the IT security manager, approves, records and time-limits. A director's seniority does not make them the policy owner, and the analyst has no authority to grant or design an exception. Refusing outright sounds safe, yet it skips the process the organization provides; routing the request lets the owner decide, perhaps with compensating controls.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because a senior leader has approved. But seniority is not authority over policy; only the policy owner can approve an exception.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting as a compromise that keeps the owner informed. But the analyst cannot design their own exception, and longer passwords are still one factor type, not MFA.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: the analyst rightly keeps MFA on. But policy provides a formal exception route, and that decision belongs to the policy owner.

tips: Eliminate: A treats seniority as policy authority, and B swaps in passwords, a single factor type, as an exception the analyst designed alone.
Final two: C beats D because exceptions are a normal, controlled part of policy; the policy owner decides, while the analyst routes and records.
Exam cue: when someone asks you to bypass a policy, neither comply nor flatly refuse; send it through the exception process to the policy owner.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 GV.PO-01 (cybersecurity policy is established, communicated and enforced); NIST CSF 2.0 ID.RA-07 (changes and exceptions are managed, assessed for risk impact, recorded and tracked)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1.3.4 Security Policies (exceptions go through a formal process: recorded, time-limited and reviewed; the policy owner approves) and 1.1.5 (two items of one factor type are not MFA). questions.question: A software firm's largest customer asks for independent proof that the firm's security management meets a recognized standard. Which approach BEST provides this?

options.A: A self-assessment against the NIST Cybersecurity Framework (CSF) 2.0
options.B: Certification against ISO/IEC 27001 by an accredited body
options.C: A penetration test report from an external testing firm
options.D: Adopting the essential safeguards of the Center for Internet Security (CIS) Controls

questions.key_concept: ISO/IEC 27001 is certifiable by accredited bodies; NIST CSF 2.0 and the CIS Controls are voluntary and carry no certification.
questions.pre_read: Notice that the customer wants independent proof about security management. Ask which option can deliver both.
questions.correct_explanation: ISO/IEC 27001 sets certifiable requirements for an information security management system, and an accredited certification body checks them independently for a stated scope. That is the proof the customer wants. A self-assessment against the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) Cybersecurity Framework is useful for describing and improving posture, but the framework is voluntary, has no certification scheme, and a self-assessment is not independent.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: CSF 2.0 is widely respected. But it is a voluntary framework with no certification, and a self-assessment is not independent proof.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because an external firm is independent. But a test probes technical weaknesses at one point in time; it does not show security management meets a standard.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the CIS Controls are widely respected. But they are a prioritized list of safeguards with no formal certification, so adopting them gives no independent proof.

tips: Eliminate: C tests technical weaknesses rather than security management, and D adopts a safeguard list that has no formal certification.
Final two: B beats A because only ISO/IEC 27001 offers certification by an accredited body; the CSF is voluntary and a self-assessment is not independent.
Exam cue: certified, independent proof of security management points to ISO/IEC 27001. CSF describes posture; CIS Controls give a starting list.

questions.question: A hospital plans to pilot an AI tool that summarizes patient notes for doctors, and the vendor says privacy law does not apply because the tool is AI. What should the security team do FIRST?

options.A: Refer the pilot to the privacy officer and legal counsel for review
options.B: Get the vendor's written confirmation that the tool meets privacy law
options.C: Let the pilot run with doctors checking every summary
options.D: Encrypt the patient notes so privacy law no longer applies

questions.key_concept: Existing privacy laws still apply to AI tools that process personal data; practitioners refer legal questions to counsel.
questions.pre_read: Notice who made the legal claim and what data the tool will touch. Then check what each option relies on.
questions.correct_explanation: Privacy law covers personal data in AI prompts, training data and outputs, whatever the vendor claims. Deciding how the law applies is not the security team's job, so the first step is to bring in the privacy officer and legal counsel before any patient data is used. A written vendor statement is tempting, but it repeats the vendor's own view, which is the claim in doubt.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting as due diligence, but the vendor already misstated the law. Its written promise does not replace the hospital's own legal review.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because human review sounds like oversight. But doctors checking summaries guards accuracy, not privacy; the vendor still receives patient notes, so lawfulness must be settled first.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because encryption protects patient data. But privacy law also governs whether and how personal data may be used; encrypting notes does not remove those duties.

tips: Eliminate: C treats doctors checking outputs as a privacy safeguard, and D treats encryption as removing legal duties; neither settles whether the processing is lawful.
Final two: A beats B because the vendor is the source of the doubtful claim; legal interpretation belongs to counsel and the privacy officer.
Exam cue: when a question turns on what the law requires, the practitioner gathers the facts and refers it to legal counsel or compliance.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 GV.OC-03 (legal, regulatory and contractual requirements, including privacy obligations, are understood and managed); ISO/IEC 27002:2022 Control 5.34 (Privacy and protection of PII)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 1.3.6 Laws and Rules That Apply to AI (privacy law still covers personal data in prompts, training data and outputs) and 1.3.2 Laws and Regulations (never interpret the law alone; bring in legal counsel). questions.question: A company's written rule says every firewall change must be approved by the network manager before it is made. How is this rule MOST accurately classified?

options.A: An administrative control over firewall changes
options.B: A technical control built into the firewall
options.C: A physical control protecting network equipment
options.D: A detective control that reveals firewall changes

questions.key_concept: Control type depends on how the control works: written rules and approvals are administrative even when their subject is technical.
questions.pre_read: Notice what form the rule takes and how it is enforced.
questions.correct_explanation: A written rule that directs how people must act is an administrative control, whatever its subject. It concerns firewalls, which makes 'technical' tempting, but the technical control is the rule set running on the firewall itself, not the document requiring approval. The approval step is preventive in function, because it stops unapproved changes before they happen; it does not detect them afterward.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the topic is firewalls. But this is a document directing people; only the rules configured on the firewall are a technical control.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the rule protects network equipment. But physical controls are tangible barriers such as locks and fences; a written approval rule is not one.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because approvals leave a record of changes. But detective controls find events after they happen; requiring approval before a change works to prevent it.

tips: Eliminate: C is for tangible barriers like locks, and D names a function, detection, that an approval required before a change does not perform.
Final two: A beats B because a written rule directs people, which makes it administrative; the firewall's running rule set is the technical control.
Exam cue: classify by how a control works, not by its subject. Documents, training and approvals are administrative, even when they concern technology.

questions.question: A clinic's server room has a door alarm that alerts staff after someone enters, but nothing stops an unauthorized person walking in. Which control should the facilities manager add to BEST close this gap?

options.A: A camera that records everyone entering through the server room door
options.B: A sign warning that the room is under surveillance
options.C: A second motion alarm mounted inside the room
options.D: A badge-controlled lock on the server room door

questions.key_concept: Match the control's function to the gap: alarms and cameras detect or deter, while locks prevent entry.
questions.pre_read: Sort the existing control by what it does. Ask which function is missing when an intruder arrives.
questions.correct_explanation: The alarm is a detective control: it reports entry after it happens. The gap is the missing preventive control, something that stops an unauthorized person getting in, and a badge-controlled lock does exactly that. A camera is the tempting runner-up because it deters and records, but footage only helps after the fact; it physically stops nobody.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: a camera deters some intruders and records who entered. But it stops nobody, so the room still has no preventive control.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because signs do discourage casual intruders. But a warning sign is a deterrent; it cannot block anyone determined to enter.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because more alarms feel like more security. But a second alarm adds detection to a room that already has it; the gap is prevention.

tips: Eliminate: B only deters, and C duplicates the detection the room already has; neither stops anyone entering.
Final two: D beats A because a lock prevents entry, while a camera deters and records but cannot physically stop an intruder.
Exam cue: first name the function that is missing (prevent, detect, correct or deter), then pick the control that performs that function.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 PE-3 (Physical Access Control); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 PE-6 (Monitoring Physical Access)

questions.question: A museum's physical security standard, owned by its head of security, requires badge readers on staff doors, but heritage law forbids altering one historic door. What should the analyst on the security team do FIRST?

options.A: Fit the badge reader anyway, because the standard is mandatory
options.B: Propose compensating controls for the standard owner's approval
options.C: Accept the risk on the museum's behalf and record it as accepted
options.D: Ask the risk owner to formally accept the risk of that door

questions.key_concept: When a required control is impossible, compensating controls approved as an exception come before accepting the remaining risk.
questions.pre_read: Notice why the standard cannot be met, and who owns the standard and the risk. Then put the options in order.
questions.correct_explanation: Law outranks an internal standard, so the reader cannot be fitted. When a required control is impossible, the first step is to find compensating controls, such as an exit alarm, a camera and a regular log review, that reduce the same risk another way. The standard's owner approves them as a recorded exception that is reviewed periodically. Risk owner acceptance comes after, for whatever risk remains.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because internal standards are mandatory. But they sit below the law; altering a protected door would break heritage law, so this option is not available.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the gap cannot be closed as required. But accepting risk commits the organization and belongs to the risk owner, not an analyst acting alone.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: the risk owner is the right person to accept risk. But accepting first skips compensating controls that could lower the risk.

tips: Eliminate: A breaks heritage law, which outranks any internal standard, and C has the analyst accept risk, a decision that belongs to the risk owner.
Final two: B beats D because compensating controls come first to lower the risk; the risk owner then accepts only what remains.
Exam cue: when a required control cannot be used, look for a compensating control through the exception process before anyone accepts the risk.

questions.question: A clinic's facilities team is fitting electronic locks to a pharmacy storeroom and to a corridor door on the fire escape route. Which power-failure settings BEST fit the two doors?

options.A: Fail-secure on both doors during any power failure
options.B: Fail-safe on both doors, so that neither door can trap anyone inside
options.C: Fail-secure on the storeroom, fail-safe on the escape-route door
options.D: Fail-safe on the storeroom, fail-secure on the escape-route door

questions.key_concept: Escape-route doors use fail-safe locks so people can get out; fail-secure locks suit storerooms that are not escape routes.
questions.pre_read: Take each door in turn: what it protects and who passes through it. Then picture the building during an outage.
questions.correct_explanation: A door on an escape route must let people out, so its lock should be fail-safe and release when power fails; life safety comes before property. The pharmacy storeroom is not an escape route, so a fail-secure lock can keep it shut and protect the stock. Fail-safe on both doors protects people but needlessly leaves the drug store open during every outage.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because it keeps the drug stock protected. But a fail-secure escape-route door could trap people during a fire or power cut; safety comes before property.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: it protects people. But nobody escapes through the storeroom, so releasing that lock in an outage exposes drugs for no safety gain.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it treats the two doors differently. But it reverses the terms: fail-secure stays locked without power, so the escape route could trap people.

tips: Eliminate: A and D both leave the escape-route door locked in an outage, which can trap people; D also mixes up the terms, since fail-secure is the setting that stays locked.
Final two: C beats B because only the escape-route door needs to release; the storeroom can stay fail-secure because nobody escapes through it.
Exam cue: protect people first, then property. Fail-safe locks go on escape routes; fail-secure locks go where nobody needs to get out.

questions.subtopic: 1.5 Professional conduct. Due care and due diligence
questions.question: A logistics firm's yearly security review found that its warehouse scanners run firmware with a known flaw, and the vendor has released a fix. Which next step BEST shows due care?

options.A: Commission a second review to confirm the flaw is real
options.B: Install the firmware update through the change process
options.C: Research how other firms have handled the same flaw
options.D: Log the firmware flaw in the risk register for review

questions.key_concept: Due diligence investigates and verifies; due care acts on what is known, as a reasonable organization would.
questions.pre_read: Notice what the review found and what the vendor has released. Then ask what each option does about it.
questions.correct_explanation: Due diligence is finding out, and the review that discovered the flaw already did that. Due care is acting on what you know as a prudent organization would, and installing the vendor's update through the change process is that action. Recording the flaw is good practice, but a register entry alone leaves the known weakness in place, and knowledge without action is what negligence claims target.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because confirming before acting sounds careful. But a second review is more due diligence; the flaw and its fix are already confirmed, so the next step is to act.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because learning from others seems prudent. But researching their responses is still investigation, which is diligence, and it delays action on a known, fixable flaw.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: recording risks is sound practice. But a register entry awaiting review leaves a known, fixable flaw in place; due care means acting on it.

tips: Eliminate: A and C keep investigating a flaw that is already confirmed; investigating and verifying are due diligence.
Final two: B beats D because due care is acting on known risks; a register entry records the flaw but leaves it unfixed.
Exam cue: diligence discovers, care carries it out. Research, assess or verify points to diligence; patch, enforce or fix points to care.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 SI-2 (Flaw Remediation); ISO/IEC 27002:2022 Control 8.8 (Management of technical vulnerabilities)

questions.question: A consulting firm's tester finds that outsiders can change a city's traffic signals, and the city asks for the flaw to be left out of the report. What is the tester's BEST response?

options.A: Honor the city's request and leave the flaw out of the report
options.B: Publish the flaw online so the city is pushed to fix it
options.C: Change the signal settings to close the flaw before reporting
options.D: Report the flaw accurately and explain its public safety risk

questions.key_concept: Serving principals never requires dishonesty; the ethical choice is honest, legal, protects people and uses proper channels.
questions.pre_read: Test each option against honesty, public safety, duty to the client and staying within authority. Look for one that passes all four.
questions.correct_explanation: Leaving out a known safety flaw would make the report dishonest and leave the public exposed, so honesty and protecting society point the same way. Serving the client diligently means giving them an accurate report and explaining the risk, not hiding it. This is decided by the facts, not by which canon is listed first: concealment fails the client too, since an unfixed flaw harms them.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because diligent service to principals is a canon. But that duty never includes a dishonest report that leaves the public at risk.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because public pressure can force a fix. But publishing before the city can fix the flaw hands attackers a way to change signals and endangers people.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because closing the flaw directly seems helpful. But testers work within the authorized scope; changing live signals goes beyond it and could cause harm on the roads.

tips: Eliminate: B exposes the flaw to attackers before it is fixed, and C changes live systems outside the tester's authorized scope.
Final two: D beats A because honest reporting serves the client and protects the public; diligent service never extends to hiding a safety flaw.
Exam cue: in ethics dilemmas, test each option against all four canons. The best answer is usually honest, legal, protective of people and done through proper channels.

questions.question: A junior analyst at a consulting firm wants a free public AI chatbot to review a client's firewall rules quickly. What is the BEST way for the analyst to proceed?

options.A: Paste the rules after removing the client's company name
options.B: Paste the rules, then have the AI's advice approved before use
options.C: Paste the rules into an AI tool approved for client data
options.D: Paste the rules, then tell the client once the review is done

questions.key_concept: Professionals keep principals' confidential data out of AI tools not approved for it, and stay accountable for AI-assisted work.
questions.pre_read: Notice what the client's firewall rules reveal. Then ask where each option sends them.
questions.correct_explanation: Firewall rules reveal how a client's network is built, which is confidential information entrusted to the firm. Pasting them into an unapproved public tool can expose it beyond the firm's control, failing the duty of diligent, competent service to the client. Removing the company name is the tempting shortcut, but the addresses and services in the rules still expose the client. An approved tool keeps the data within agreed protections.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: it reduces what is shared. But the rules themselves still expose the client's network details to a tool nobody approved for them.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because approving AI advice before use is part of competent work. But it does nothing about the client data already sent to an unapproved service.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because telling the client is honest. But afterward is too late; the data has already left the firm's control without permission.

tips: Eliminate: B checks the output but still leaks the input, and D informs the client only after their data has left the firm's control.
Final two: C beats A because removing a name does not remove what the rules reveal; client data belongs only in tools approved for it.
Exam cue: with AI tools, protect the principal's data first. Use tools approved for that data, verify the output, and stay honest about how work was produced.

questions.question: A security analyst is asked by their manager to score three firewall vendors, and their spouse works in sales at one of them. What should the analyst do FIRST?

options.A: Disclose the relationship to the manager before scoring begins
options.B: Score the three vendors fairly and keep the relationship private
options.C: Score the spouse's employer lower to offset any bias
options.D: Score as normal and leave the final choice to the manager

questions.key_concept: Conflicts of interest are disclosed before acting, so others can decide how to manage them; private fairness is not enough.
questions.pre_read: Notice the personal link in the scenario, and when in the task each option deals with it.
questions.correct_explanation: A conflict of interest exists when personal ties could sway, or seem to sway, a professional judgment. The analyst should disclose it before scoring so the manager can decide how to handle it, perhaps by reassigning the work. Scoring fairly in private is the tempting runner-up, but the analyst cannot judge their own bias, and a hidden link damages trust even when the scores are honest.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: fairness is the goal. But a conflict must be disclosed so others can manage it; privately promising to be fair still hides it.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it seems to cancel out bias. But marking a vendor down because of a relationship is its own bias, and the conflict stays hidden.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the manager makes the final choice. But the analyst's scores shape that choice, so the conflict still matters and must be disclosed.

tips: Eliminate: C swaps one bias for another, and D wrongly assumes a conflict matters only to whoever makes the final decision.
Final two: A beats B because conflicts of interest are handled by disclosure; nobody can reliably judge their own bias in private.
Exam cue: for a personal link to a vendor, candidate or case, disclose it to your manager before acting, and let them decide.

questions.question: A hardware store's owner classifies its product catalog as public, and orders stop whenever the catalog is unavailable to the online shop. How should the security team MOST accurately rate this data?

options.A: Low sensitivity and high criticality
options.B: High sensitivity and high criticality
options.C: High sensitivity and low criticality
options.D: Low sensitivity and low criticality

questions.key_concept: Sensitivity is the protection an owner says data needs, mostly from disclosure; criticality is how much the organization depends on it.
questions.pre_read: Ask two separate questions about the catalog: what harm if outsiders read it, and what harm if nobody can reach it?
questions.correct_explanation: Sensitivity reflects how much protection the owner says information needs, mostly from disclosure; criticality reflects how much the business depends on it. The owner classed the catalog as public, so outsiders reading it does no harm: low sensitivity. Orders stop without it: high criticality. Rating it high on both, the runner-up, mistakes business importance for secrecy; the catalog matters because the shop needs it, not because it is confidential.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: the catalog is vital to the shop, so it feels sensitive. But its owner classed it as public; its importance is criticality, not secrecy.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because confidentiality is the goal people think of first. But the catalog is public and orders depend on it, so both ratings are reversed.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because public data seems to need little protection. But orders stop whenever the catalog is unavailable, so the business depends on it heavily.

tips: Eliminate: C reverses both ratings, and D rates criticality low, though criticality measures dependence and orders stop without the catalog.
Final two: A beats B because a public catalog needs no protection from readers; its importance to orders makes it critical, not sensitive.
Exam cue: rate sensitivity and criticality separately. Public data can be critical, and secret data can be rarely needed.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-30 Rev. 1 Appendix B Glossary (criticality and sensitivity); NIST SP 800-12 Rev. 1 Section 1.4 (Important Terminology: confidentiality, integrity, availability)

questions.question: A city's river sensors send readings to a flood-warning server, and its engineering team wants the server to reject readings that were altered or sent by a fake sensor. Which control BEST fits?

options.A: A plain hash of each reading, sent along with the reading
options.B: A keyed hash using a secret each sensor shares with the server
options.C: Encryption of each reading with the server's public key
options.D: A timestamped server log entry for every sensor reading

questions.key_concept: Integrity asks whether data changed; authenticity asks who sent it. A keyed hash shows both; anyone can recompute a plain hash.
questions.pre_read: The engineers want two things: proof a reading is unchanged, and proof it came from a real sensor. Check each option against both.
questions.correct_explanation: A keyed hash, such as an HMAC, can only be made by someone holding the secret key, so the server can confirm a reading is unchanged and came from a genuine sensor. The plain hash is the runner-up: it reveals accidental damage, but an attacker who alters or fakes a reading simply computes a new hash to match. A digital signature is not needed, as nobody must prove origin to outsiders.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: a hash does reveal changes. But it uses no key, so anyone who alters or forges a reading can compute a matching hash.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because encryption feels like full protection. But anyone can use the server's public key, so it cannot show who sent a reading.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because logs support accountability. But a log records what arrived; it cannot tell a genuine reading from an altered or forged one.

tips: Eliminate: C relies on encryption, which protects secrecy with a key anyone can use, and D records readings without checking them.
Final two: B beats A because only holders of the secret key can make a valid keyed hash; anyone can recompute a plain hash.
Exam cue: 'has it changed?' asks integrity; 'who sent it?' asks authenticity. A key-based check answers both; a plain hash answers only the first.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-12 Rev. 1 Section 9.1.2 (Integrity); NIST SP 800-12 Rev. 1 Section 9.1.3.1 (Secret Key Electronic Signatures); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 SC-8(1) (Transmission Confidentiality and Integrity | Cryptographic Protection)

questions.question: A florist's online shop runs on one server, and a failed disk took it offline for a day, though its backups were intact. What should the IT lead propose to BEST avoid another day offline?

options.A: Add a standby server that takes over automatically
options.B: Encrypt the server's disks so stolen data stays unreadable
options.C: Back up the shop's data every hour instead of nightly
options.D: Turn on file integrity monitoring for the shop's web pages

questions.key_concept: Availability controls must fit the cause of downtime: redundancy removes single points of failure, while backups recover lost data.
questions.pre_read: Find what actually caused the outage, and which security goal it harmed, before matching a control to it.
questions.correct_explanation: The outage came from the only server failing, a single point of failure. A second server that takes over automatically removes it, so a disk fault no longer stops sales. More frequent backups, the runner-up, also sound like availability, but backups restore lost data, and the shop lost none; it simply had nothing to run on while the disk was replaced.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because encryption is a core safeguard. But it protects confidentiality, and the problem here was a shop that could not run.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: backups support recovery. But the backups were already intact; more of them would not keep the shop running while the server was down.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because monitoring sounds protective. But it detects unauthorized changes to files, an integrity check; it cannot keep a failed server running.

tips: Eliminate: B protects confidentiality and D detects changes for integrity; neither keeps the shop running when hardware fails.
Final two: A beats C because the shop lost no data, only its one server; redundancy keeps service running, while backups restore lost data.
Exam cue: for availability, find the cause of downtime first. Redundancy answers single points of failure, filtering answers floods, backups answer lost data.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 PR.IR-03 (mechanisms are implemented to achieve resilience requirements in normal and adverse situations); NIST SP 800-12 Rev. 1 Section 1.4 (Important Terminology: confidentiality, integrity, availability)

questions.question: A logistics firm's warehouse staff sign in with a password, then type a six-digit code shown by an authenticator app on their enrolled phone. Which factor type does the code MOST accurately represent?

options.A: Something you know, because staff type the code in
options.B: Something you are, because each phone is linked to one person
options.C: Something you have, because it proves staff hold the phone
options.D: Not a factor, because the app creates the code, not the person

questions.key_concept: A factor is classed by what it proves: a code from an enrolled device proves possession, so it is something you have.
questions.pre_read: Ask what an attacker would need to produce the code: knowledge in someone's head, a body trait or a particular object.
questions.correct_explanation: A factor is classed by what it proves, not by how it is entered. The code is generated from a secret stored on the enrolled phone, so producing it proves the user holds that phone: something you have. Something you know, the runner-up, is tempting because the code is typed, but nobody memorizes it; whoever holds the phone can read it without knowing anything.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the code is typed like a password. But nobody memorizes it; it comes from the enrolled phone, so it proves possession.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the phone is personal. But something you are means a body trait, such as a fingerprint; owning a device is possession.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the user does not choose the code. But the app holds a secret enrolled for that user, so a valid code proves they hold the device.

tips: Eliminate: B mistakes owning a device for a body trait, and D misses that a code from an enrolled device is a factor in its own right.
Final two: C beats A because factors are classed by what they prove; the code proves the phone is in hand, not that anything was memorized.
Exam cue: classify a factor by what an attacker would need: a secret in someone's head (know), an object (have) or a body trait (are).
